title: Week 1: Defining the Depth Function & Infrastructure Setup
text: I kicked off my 16 week undergraduate research term this week under the supervision of Dr. Alexandre Leblanc by defining the core scope of our project: the statistical and computational challenges of Data Depth. While the week was heavily focused on literature review, foundational theory, and establishing the technical infrastructure to document the progress over the summer, it also allowed me to pinpoint the applications of this concept that I am most interested in exploring. Specifically, I want to investigate how data depth can be used for robust outlier detection under missing data. Is there a depth method that can isolate high quality data points from the noise? Can the approach be generalised to higher dimensions?

title: Week 3: Clarifying Tukey Depth & Debugging Sweep Algorithm
text:
Abstract
This week was dedicated to resolving the calculation errors in my Tukey depth algorithm from Week 2, which ultimately required a much deeper dive into the underlying geometry. I discovered that my bugs weren’t just syntactical. They stemmed from a gap in understanding of the Tukey depth measure, which resulted in unconsciously mixing two equivalent, but geometrically distinct, definitions of Tukey depth. By decoupling the “Halfspace” view from the “Projection” view, I was able to fix the initial-count logic of my sweep algorithm and resolve a persistent off-by-one boundary error. With an algorithm setup for Tukey Depth finally in place, I am now naturally transitioning into a deeper dive in the Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) depth as the two share many similarities.



Visualizing Two Views of Tukey Depth





Side by side plots that depict two different ways to interpret and calculate Tukey Depth




While these two geometric interpretations look completely different, they are mathematically identical. Realizing how they align was the key aspect to fixing the error in my algorithm and strengthening my understanding.



Theoretical Foundations: Understanding the Definitions

Core Concepts: The graphs above will play a vital role in understanding the formal definitions of these views.

Projection View (Left Side): As suggested by (Tukey 1975) and explained in Dr. Leblanc’s instructional materials, a measure of the depth of a point \(y\) given a sample \(X = (X_1,...,X_n)'\) in 1D is \(D_1(y,X) = \min(\#\{i : X_i \le y\}, \#\{i : X_i \ge y\})\) and this can be generalised to \(d\) dimensions as: \[D_d(y,X) = \min_{||u|| = 1} D_1(u'y, X(u))\] where \(X(u) = (u'X_1,...,u'X_n)'\) is the projected sample. Let’s unfold this definition with the help of the graph above.

The light blue line represents one possible directional vector. The dashed lines show how the 2D data cloud projects onto that 1D light blue line. The red dot represents our query point’s projected position onto the 1D line. To find the depth on this specific line, we simply count the green dots on the left side and the right side of the red dot, and take the smaller of the two. The final depth of this query point is the minimum 1D depth observed over all directional vectors. This method reduces the multivariate problem into a series of univariate problems.

Halfspace View (Right Side): (Rousseeuw and Ruts 1998) outlines that the halfspace Tukey depth of a point \(y\) relative to a dataset \(X\) is defined as: \[D(y,X) = \min_{H} \#\{i ; x_i \in H\}\] where H ranges over all closed halfspaces where the boundary line passes through \(y\). Let’s unfold this definition with the help of the graph above.

The blue arrow represents the line from the query point ‘y’ (red dot) to one of the data points in the sample. The dashed line shows the result of extending this line to infinity. We observe that this line divides the plane into two spaces, left and right. To find the depth for this specific line, we just count the number of dots (sample points in black) on the left side and the right side of the line, and take the smaller number. The final depth of this query point is the minimum depth observed over all possible lines through the query point.


Literature Context: Consulted (Tukey 1975) and (Rousseeuw and Ruts 1998) specifically to extract and understand the definitions discussed above.




Methodological Pivots & Insights
Last week, my single point Tukey algorithm was producing results that completely mismatched the verified ddalpha package output. I spent the week tracing the variables and discovered two distinct logic errors.

Error 1: Incorrect Initial Count (Mixing Definitions)

The Problem: The sweep algorithm I am writing is strictly based on the Projection definition. However, when I wrote the code to calculate the initial count (the number of points that project on the right side before the angular sweep begins from 0 to 360 degrees), I accidentally wrote logic based on the Halfspace definition. I was counting the total number of observations in the top-half (positive y-axis), instead of counting the total number of observations in the right-half (positive x-axis), which is all the points that project on the right before the sweep begins.
The Fix: I was implementing one definition but using the boundary rules of the other. Once I realized that the initial count simply represents all points that initially project onto the right side of the directional vector at angle 0, I rewrote the initialization chunk, and the sweep angles finally aligned.

Error 2: Off-By-One

The Problem: Even after fixing the sweep, my depth was constantly exactly one less than the ddalpha depth. However, this only happened for in sample points (points that existed in the dataset). When I tested an out of sample point, my code matched ddalpha perfectly.
The Fix: Dr. Leblanc helped me understand that it comes down to the definition of a closed halfspace vs an open halfspace. A closed halfspace includes the boundary line itself. In my original logic, I didn’t explicitly count the target point in the left/right totals because I assumed that adding 1 to both sides wouldn’t change which side was the minimum. While it is true that adding 1 to both sides doesn’t change which side is smaller, it definitely changes the final numerical depth value. Because the target point sits on the boundary, it must be counted if considering closed halfspaces. Understanding this helped me realise that ddalpha uses closed halfspaces whereas I implemented the open halfspace definition. Thus, this was not so much of an error but rather a difference in implementations.




Computational Implementation

Infrastructure: Continuing in R, utilizing the ddalpha package primarily for output verification.
Algorithmic Complexity: By sorting the projected angles before starting the circular sweep, the exact computation of the bivariate Tukey depth was achieved in \(O(n \log n)\) time.
The Corrected Logic (The Initial Count): Following the correct logic of the projection approach, the algorithm isolates the exact number of points projecting onto the right side of the initial directional vector at angle 0 before the sweep begins.


# BUG FIX: Implementing correct projection logic
# Correctly isolating the initial count of points on the right side of the 0-degree vector

#function to check if we are in the right-half (to find initial count)
checkQuad = function(x){
  if(x > 0){
    answer = 1
  } else{
    answer = 0
  }
  return(answer)
}

#calculating starting depth (i.e. initial count)
minDepth = 0
right_count = 0
n = nrow(df)
i = 1
while(i <= nrow(df)){
  if(checkQuad(shiftedMPG[i]) == 1){
    right_count = right_count + 1
  }
  i = i + 1
}
left_count = n - right_count
minDepth = min(left_count,right_count)


Note: The complete, executable R script for the bivariate Tukey sweep algorithm is available in the project repository.




Future Work

Optimize the R syntax in the algorithm by replacing standard loops with vectorized operations to better handle larger datasets and eliminate computational bottlenecks.
Scale the corrected single-point Tukey algorithm to compute depth for an entire dataset.
Check how the algorithm scales as \(n \rightarrow \infty\)
Begin literature review and implementation for Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) depth.






References

Rousseeuw, Peter J., and Ida Ruts. 1998. “CONSTRUCTING THE BIVARIATE TUKEY MEDIAN.” Statistica Sinica 8 (3): 827–39. http://www.jstor.org/stable/24306466.


Tukey, John W. 1975. “Mathematics and the Picturing of Data.” Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians 2: 523–31.

title: Week 4: Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) Depth and Monte Carlo Approximations
text:
Abstract
With the geometrical foundation of the bivariate Tukey sweep algorithm solidified last week, my focus shifted toward Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) depth. While Tukey depth is a powerful depth measure, finding the minimum univariate depth over all possible projections makes Tukey Depth difficult to compute. IRW depth resolves this by averaging the univariate depths across all projections rather than taking the absolute minimum. Since there are no built-in R packages like ddalpha that help verify IRW computations, I implemented the algorithm three distinct ways upon Dr. Leblanc’s recommendation. My implementations range from an exact geometric calculation to a pure Monte Carlo approximation, which helped ensure the mathematical correctness of my results.



Visualizing IRW Depth





A simple toy example to help understand how IRW Depth is computed.




In this highly simplified example, let’s assume there are a total of 4 projections. Now, Tukey depth measure tells us to find the minimum univariate depth over all projections. So, the Tukey depth of our query point would be \(2\). On the other hand, IRW depth is computed by averaging the univariate depth over all projections. Thus, the IRW depth of the query point is \(\frac{5+5+2+3}{4} = 3.75\). Hence, evaluating IRW is simply a matter of casting directional vectors, finding the univariate Tukey depth for each, and averaging the results.



Theoretical Foundations: Tukey vs IRW Depth

Core Concepts: While IRW depth shares much of its structure with Tukey depth, the core difference lies in how the final value is extracted from the projections.

The Tukey Shortcoming: Recall that Tukey depth takes the absolute minimum 1D depth across all possible projections. Since we strictly look for the minimum, it outputs a step function, which could result in many points sharing the same rank/depth value. Moreover, standard calculus techniques fail when optimizing a step function which further makes Tukey Depth difficult to compute.
The IRW Advantage: IRW depth solves this by taking the average (or integral) of the 1D depths across all uniformly distributed projection directions. By averaging the depths rather than isolating the minimum, IRW provides a strictly decreasing, smooth continuous depth function from the center outward. Moreover, using this integration approach makes it easy to approximate the depth of a point in higher dimensions through Monte Carlo techniques. (Ramsay et al. 2019)

Literature Context: As extracted from (Ramsay et al. 2019) and simplified by Dr. Leblanc in his research talk slides, the IRW Depth of a point \(y\) with respect to a sample \(X = (X_1,...,X_n)'\) of \(R^d\) is given by \[D_{IRW}(y, X) = \frac{1}{Area(S^{d-1})} \int_{S^{d-1}}D_1(u'y,X(u))du\] where \(S^{d-1} = \{u \in R^d:\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert = 1\}\), \(D_1(u'y,X(u))\) is the 1D Tukey depth, and \(X(u)=(u'X_1,...,u'X_n)'\) is the projected sample.




Computational Implementation & Verification Strategy

The Verification Challenge: One of the immediate hurdles this week was the lack of a built-in verification tool. Unlike Tukey depth, there is no function for IRW depth within the ddalpha package (or any other standard R libraries that I explored). This meant I could not simply run my algorithm and compare the output to an answer key. To ensure the mathematical integrity of my code, I had to come up with a robust verification strategy relying on algorithmic independence. Dr. Leblanc suggested leveraging the convergence property of Monte Carlo simulations to verify the code. If an exact geometrical approach and a randomized approximation approach yield the same value, the implementation is successful. To achieve this, I implemented IRW depth in three distinct ways:

Exact IRW Depth (The Sweep Method): For this implementation, I referenced the approach of representing IRW depth as a weighted average of a set of univariate Tukey ranks outlined in (Ramsay et al. 2019). This approach relies on the fact that the univariate depth is constant over distinct patches. Leveraging the sorted angular sweep from Week 3, I computed the exact IRW depth by tracking the boundaries where the depth changes. Instead of keeping track of the absolute minimum, I stored every univariate depth observed in a vector. I calculated the angular slice size (the weight of the total pie) for each depth, and summed them using the following logic: \[D_{IRW Exact} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} w_i d_i\] where \(w_i\) is the size of the angular slice (proportion of projections out of total), and \(d_i\) is the depth observed in that slice.
Semi-Randomized IRW (Sweep + Randomization): Using the exact slices computed above, I introduced randomization. I generated \(m\) random angles (\(\theta\)) uniformly. For each \(\theta\), the algorithm determined which angular slice it landed in and stored the corresponding pre-computed depth for that slice. The final depth was the average of these \(m\) depths.
Pure Monte Carlo Approximation (No Pre-Setup): Since IRW depth requires computing an average, there is a very simple Monte Carlo algorithm for approximating the depth of a point. For this implementation, we remove the angular sweep entirely. Similar to the strategy explained by (Durocher et al. 2017), this is purely a brute force implementation. I generated \(m\) random projection vectors. For each vector, the data was projected onto the line, and the 1D depth was calculated. The final IRW depth is the average of the depths computed for all \(m\) projections. The law of large numbers guarantees that this algorithm does converge to the exact value (Ramsay et al. 2019) as computed in implementation 1 as \(m \rightarrow \infty\), and the graph below confirms this result.







Monte Carlo Approximation of IRW Converging to the exact IRW Depth.




The grey dashed line represents the depth computed under the exact implementation and we observe that after being chaotic for roughly 1000 directions, the approximation starts converging to the exact value (i.e. the dashed line.)

The Result: All three implementations successfully converged to the same depth value. As Dr. Leblanc noted, because the exact implementation and the Monte Carlo implementation are independent of one another, their depth values matching acts as a reliable validation tool for the code.
Note: The complete, executable R script for all three implementations is available in the project repository.




Future Work

Optimize the R syntax in the algorithm to eliminate computational bottlenecks.
Check how the algorithm scales as \(n \rightarrow \infty\). Confirm runtime matches the theoretical expectation.
Research curiosity - Explore implementation of IRW logic in 3D space.
Begin literature review and implementation for Simplicial depth.






References

Durocher, Stephane, Alexandre Leblanc, and Matthew Skala. 2017. “The Projection Median as a Weighted Average.” J. Comput. Geom. 8: 78–104. https://api.semanticscholar.org/CorpusID:4936625.


Ramsay, Kelly, Stéphane Durocher, and Alexandre Leblanc. 2019. “Integrated Rank-Weighted Depth.” J. Multivar. Anal. (USA) 173 (C): 51–69. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmva.2019.02.001.

title: Week 2: First Computations in R - Implementing Mahalanobis & Tukey Depth
text:
Abstract
This week marked the transition from understanding mathematical theory to applying it through computational implementation. The primary goal was to have a functioning algorithm, leaving runtime optimization for later iterations. After reviewing Dr. Leblanc’s notes to solidify the core geometry, I wrote my first R scripts to compute Mahalanobis depth (for an entire dataset) using matrix algebra and Tukey depth (for a single point), understanding why simple distance measurements fail in multivariate space, and learning two different but equivalent ways to compute Tukey depth. While built-in R functions made computing Mahalanobis depth straightforward, I spent the vast majority of my time struggling with the geometric complexities of Tukey depth.



Theoretical Foundations: Two Approaches to Computing Depth

The Core Concept: This week focused on two different methods for calculating depth.

Mahalanobis depth is based on Mahalanobis distance. It relies on the covariance matrix to measure how central a point is relative to the distribution’s shape and spread.
Tukey (halfspace) depth takes a geometric approach. Using the projection interpretation, it determines depth of a point by evaluating the minimum number of data points whose orthogonal projections fall to one side of the origin across all possible directional vectors.

Literature Context: Relied primarily on Dr. Leblanc’s notes to solidify the theoretical foundation and understand computational geometry via animations. Briefly referenced (Mosler and Mozharovskyi 2022) for an introduction to Mahalanobis Depth and its properties.
Research Curiosities: (Mosler and Mozharovskyi 2022) demonstrates that Mahalanobis depth can be calculated exactly in \(O(n)\) time for any number of dimensions. However, because this depth method is not robust to outliers, it is unreliable for many modern applications. I am naturally curious to explore robustified versions of Mahalanobis depth. What computational trade-offs must we make when transitioning from the standard version to a robust one?



Visualizing the Output


View the Code to Generate the Scatterplot
#two points mentioned in the write-up
obser1 = data.frame(x=22.8, y=2.320)
obser2 = data.frame(x=26.0, y=2.140)

#plot data to observe how the depth changes
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(updatedDF, aes(x = updatedDF$mpg, y = updatedDF$wt, 
                      label = updatedDF$mhlnbsDepth_2d)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_point(aes(x = obser1$x, y = obser1$y), colour = "red")+
  geom_point(aes(x = obser2$x, y = obser2$y), colour = "blue")+
  annotate( #plotting the direction of maximum variance
    "segment", 
    x = 24, y = 2.75,     
    xend = 29, yend = 2.1,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")),
    color = "grey", 
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate( #plotting the direction of minimum variance
    "segment", 
    x = 23, y = 2.75,     
    xend = 21, yend = 2.2,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")),
    color = "darkgreen", 
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_text(color = "darkred",
                           size = 1.5, vjust = -1)+
  labs(x = "mpg", y = "wt")





Scatter plot showing the Mahalanobis Depth of each data point.





Observation: The most fascinating takeaway from the above Mahalanobis visualization was observing a highly counter intuitive result. I found a specific point (the red point) that was physically closer to the geometric center of the data as per Euclidean distance, yet it had a lower Mahalanobis depth than the blue point that was physically further away.
Understanding Why?: Upon further discussion with Dr. Leblanc, I learnt that this is because the data distribution is elliptical (due to the two variables being correlated) rather than perfectly circular, and depth is determined by the data’s covariance structure.

The First Eigenvector (Maximum Variance): The blue point lies in this direction (as shown by the grey arrow). Because the data spreads widely here due to high variance, a point can be physically distant but still maintain a high depth.
The Second Eigenvector (Minimum Variance): The red point lies in this direction (as shown by the green arrow). Because the data is tightly clustered here due to low variance, moving even slightly away from the center causes the depth to drop drastically.





Computational Implementation

Infrastructure & Tools: Exclusively coded in R due to its large variety of built-in matrix operations, and the ddalpha package, which provided functions to verify my algorithm’s outputs.
The Approach:

Mahalanobis: Due to the simple structure of the formula and the built-in matrix operation functions in R, implementing the algorithm was straightforward and easily extendable to the entire dataset across higher dimensions.
Tukey: Of the two definitions, I opted to implement the projection interpretation using a sweep style algorithm. To ensure mathematical accuracy and clarity in understanding, I isolated the algorithm to compute the depth of a single sample point only.





Methodological Pivots & Insights
Implementing Tukey depth required a major conceptual pivot. My initial idea to interpret the projection definition was to rotate a line in one degree increments to find the minimum depth.
After discussing this with Dr. Leblanc, I realized that this “grid approach” was fundamentally flawed. It only provides an approximation for the depth and not the exact answer. If the true minimum is achieved at a fraction of a degree, the increment approach misses it entirely. Furthermore, it scales poorly as sample sizes grow.
I abandoned the grid approach in favor of the sweep algorithm. Instead of rotating a line, we use linear algebra to compute the exact angles where a point switches from projecting on the right versus the left. By keeping track of the action to be taken at each angle, we can sweep the sorted list of angles one by one, tracking the absolute minimum. This pivot moved my algorithm from an inefficient approximation to computing the exact Tukey depth in 2D.


Current Roadblock

The Unresolved Bug: While the transition to the sweep algorithm was conceptually successful, my current R script for the single point Tukey depth is producing an answer that is different from the one computed by the ddalpha package function, even after accounting for the normalization.
My Hypothesis: I suspect there is a flaw in how I am tracking the initial right count (i.e. number of points that project on the right of the origin) before we start sweeping the list going from 0 to 360. I have isolated the code chunk that counts the initial count and plan to debug it next week after consulting Dr. Leblanc.




Future Work

Debug the logic in the Tukey algorithm to resolve the current calculation error.
Scale the corrected single point Tukey algorithm to compute depth for an entire dataset.
Introduction to “Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) Depth”.






References

Mosler, Karl, and Pavlo Mozharovskyi. 2022. “Choosing Among Notions of Multivariate Depth Statistics.” Statistical Science 37 (3): 348–68. https://doi.org/10.1214/21-STS827.
